title: Measures To Restrict Stockpiling of Polysilicon and Polysilicon Derivatives Under Proclamation 11052
note: F: A temporary rule, "effective September 22, 2026, through December 3, 2026", that stops importers bringing in polysilicon products "in volumes substantially greater than their historic averages" before the Section 232 measures start on December 4, 2026. New importers (registered on or after August 6, 2026) get weekly caps such as "HTSUS 2804.61.00: 12 kg"; waivers are possible, with Commerce aiming to answer "within 14 days". F (Proclamation 11052, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/11/2026-16400/adjusting-imports-of-polysilicon-and-its-derivatives-into-the-united-states): from December 4, minimum import prices of "$21 per kilogram for polysilicon" and "$100 per kilogram for polysilicon ingots and wafers", plus a "15 percent ad valorem rate of duty" on derivatives. Real for chip supply but small for the watchlist: the stockpiling rule is mostly procedural and aimed at solar importers; the lasting cost from December 4 falls on US fabs importing polysilicon or wafers (Foundry and packaging: INTC, TSM Arizona; Memory: MU; indirectly ENTG). Not yet confirmed which tariff codes cover chip wafers versus solar cells, and no watchlist company has quantified exposure. No card changes today.

title: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
note: F (Federal Register abstract in data.json): an interim final rule that adds licence requirements for exports, reexports or in-country transfers 'to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau' (D:5 includes China). R (law-firm summaries, not the rule text: Morgan Lewis https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/11/commerce-targets-remote-access-to-advanced-semiconductors-in-new-interim-final-rule ; Steptoe https://www.steptoe.com/en/news-publications/international-compliance-blog/bis-targets-data-center-remote-access-and-imposes-steeper-requirements-on-foundries-and-osats.html ; Pillsbury https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/commerce-restricts-remote-access-advanced-chips.html): the trigger is data centres giving more than 12 million aggregate TPP (total processing performance, a chip-power measure); it adds country licence needs for Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand with a reporting exclusion for US-headquartered buyers; it puts licence duties on foundries and OSATs (outsourced packaging and test firms) making chips for non-approved designers; and it formally rescinds the AI Diffusion Rule. Real issue: it closes the 'rent the GPUs offshore' route for Chinese firms and adds paperwork and delay to Southeast Asian data-centre sales (NVDA, AMD, AVGO, SMCI, DELL, neoclouds such as CRWV and NBIS) and screening work for TSM, INTC foundry and AMKR. Rescinding the Diffusion Rule lowers risk elsewhere, so the net effect is uncertain until the rule text and company comments are read. No card changes today; the Federal Register page could not be opened from this session, so the R items must be checked against the rule text.
